The code is **JAUS**. I found it by working through the weights by hand, without running anything.

**Where it is hidden.** Each cell is always exactly one of three things: mover's piece, opponent's piece or empty. So for any hidden unit, the three input weights tied to cell k (inputs k, 9+k and 18+k) always add up to the same total. You can add any constant c to all three and subtract 9c from the bias, and the network gives exactly the same output. That is a place to store data that never changes how the network plays.

**What stands out.** For most hidden units, the per-cell sum S = W1[j][k] + W1[j][9+k] + W1[j][18+k] varies a lot from cell to cell. In four units, which are evenly spaced 8 apart, it is the same for all nine cells, to within ±0.001:

| Hidden unit | Per-cell sum (all 9 cells) | Letter (A=1) |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | 0.10 | J |
| 13 | 0.01 | A |
| 21 | 0.21 | U |
| 29 | 0.19 | S |

For example, unit 13, cell 3: −1.958 + 1.978 − 0.011 = 0.009. Unit 21, cell 0: −0.954 + 1.347 − 0.182 = 0.211. Every unit I checked outside these four fails this test within its first two or three cells.

**Two assumptions in the decoding.** I read each constant as hundredths with A=1, so 0.01 is A. Counting from A=0 instead would make 0.00 the code for A, which can't be seen, so A=1 is the sensible reading. I also put the letters in hidden-unit order, 5, 13, 21, 29. JAUS isn't a word, but the pattern is too clean to be chance.

CODE: JAUS
